subject: chemistry-1
question: In a teaching demonstration, hydrochloric acid is neutralized by calcium hydroxide: 2 HCl + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCl2 + 2 H2O. How many moles of Ca(OH)2 are required to neutralize 0.4 mol of HCl completely?

options.text: 0.2 mol, because each mole of Ca(OH)2 supplies two moles of hydroxide
0.4 mol, because an acid and a base always neutralize in a 1:1 ratio
0.1 mol, because each of the two hydroxide ions neutralizes two moles of acid
0.8 mol, because each mole of HCl requires two moles of the base

explanation:
The balanced equation sets a 2:1 mole ratio of HCl to Ca(OH)2, so 0.4 mol HCl requires 0.4 / 2 = 0.2 mol of the base. Each formula unit of Ca(OH)2 releases two hydroxide ions, so one mole of it neutralizes two moles of a monoprotic acid such as HCl. Assuming every acid-base pairing is 1:1 is a frequent misconception that produces a twofold error in the amount of base.

ELI-10: Neutralization pairs one H+ with one OH-. HCl delivers one H+ per formula unit, while Ca(OH)2 delivers two OH- per formula unit. So each unit of base can handle two units of this acid, and you need only half as many moles of base as acid: 0.4 divided by 2 is 0.2 mol.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
